text: Identity-plus-context is the real perimeter, and device is one of the biggest pieces of that context — easy to underweight if you're only thinking about users and passwords. This lesson is about why device compliance has to sit inside the access decision itself, not off to the side as a separate IT checklist.

Picture two sign-ins with the exact same username, password, and even a passing MFA challenge. One comes from a company laptop that's encrypted, patched, enrolled in Intune, and reporting a clean posture. The other comes from an unknown personal device with no management agent and no visibility into whether it's already compromised. The identity signal looks identical in both — a correctly authenticated user — but the real risk is not the same at all. An access decision that only asks who this is is missing half the picture.

Intune compliance policies define what compliant actually means, per platform: a minimum OS version, disk encryption like BitLocker or FileVault, a device password or PIN, no jailbreak or root, and a threat level from a connected endpoint-protection signal staying under a configured threshold. Intune evaluates a device against those rules on a recurring basis and reports one simple result back to Microsoft Entra ID — compliant or not. The granular rules live in Intune; Conditional Access only consumes that resulting signal.

It's worth being precise, because Conditional Access exposes two separate device grant controls that answer different questions. Require Hybrid Azure AD joined device asks where the device came from and who provisioned it. Require device to be marked as compliant asks whether Intune considers it healthy right now. A device can be hybrid-joined but no longer compliant if its encryption got disabled later — treating these as interchangeable is a common design mistake worth catching in an architecture review.

The reason this has to live inside the access decision, not beside it, is timing. Compliance state has to be available at the exact moment access is requested, combined with identity and risk in the same evaluation, so a non-compliant device gets blocked on this request, not flagged for review next week. A signal only checked periodically and out of band isn't verifying explicitly — it's auditing after the fact. Next lesson puts this signal, PIM, and Conditional Access together into one identity fabric that reaches into AWS too.
